title: Day two of chemotherapy
objective: Recognize oncologic emergencies the nurse must report at once, such as tumor lysis syndrome with its high potassium, high phosphate and low calcium

brief.situation: 06:00 on an oncology unit. You are Mr. Vega's nurse. He is 42, on day 2 of induction chemotherapy for a high-grade lymphoma with a large tumor burden. His 05:00 labs have posted and he says his legs are cramping and his fingers tingle.
handover: Orders: IV hydration at the ordered rate, strict intake and output, allopurinol, labs every 6 hours. His maintenance IV bag has potassium added.
Urine output overnight: 120, then 80, then 40 mL an hour.

Unit policy: oncologic emergencies (including tumor lysis syndrome) are reported to the oncology provider at once; the RN may place the patient on telemetry and stop potassium-containing fluid while calling.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each assessment takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

Peaked T waves on the strip.
Leg cramps, tingling around his mouth and fingers, a positive Chvostek sign: low calcium.
Intake 3.2 L, output 1.1 L over 12 hours; output falling hour by hour.

why.question: What is happening on day 2 of his chemotherapy, why is it an emergency, and what do you do?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: Tumor lysis syndrome after starting chemotherapy for a high-grade lymphoma: hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, hyperuricemia and AKI; hyperkalemia with peaked T waves threatens a fatal dysrhythmia, and low calcium causes cramps and tingling.
parts.modelAnswer: This is tumor lysis syndrome: the chemo is breaking down a lot of tumor fast, flooding him with potassium, phosphate and uric acid, which drops his calcium and hurts his kidneys. His potassium of 6.4 with peaked T waves can cause a fatal rhythm, and his cramps and tingling are the low calcium.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Reports to the oncology provider at once; telemetry; stops potassium-containing fluid; gives ordered treatment; strict intake and output; does not wait for rounds.
parts.modelAnswer: Call the oncology provider now, put him on telemetry and stop the potassium in his IV. Give the ordered hyperkalemia treatment and rasburicase, keep strict intake and output, and don't wait for 09:00 rounds.

arrest.headline: Arrest
arrest.body: Tumor lysis syndrome after chemotherapy brings high potassium, high phosphate, low calcium and kidney injury. It is reported at once, with telemetry and potassium sources stopped.

reported.headline: Reported and treated
reported.body: You recognized tumor lysis syndrome from the lab pattern, put him on telemetry, stopped the potassium and reported within minutes. That is the expert path.

scoring.modelReasoning: On day 2 of chemotherapy for a high-grade lymphoma with a large tumor burden, a potassium of 6.4 with peaked T waves, high phosphate and uric acid, low calcium with cramps, tingling and a positive Chvostek sign, a doubled creatinine and falling output are tumor lysis syndrome: an oncologic emergency. Hyperkalemia is the most immediate danger. Put him on telemetry, stop the potassium-containing fluid, report to the oncology provider at once rather than at rounds, give the ordered hyperkalemia treatment and rasburicase, and keep strict intake and output.
